content:
For a while now I’ve been watching people make motion graphics with AI. Since Opus 5.5 came out, every week someone shows up with a product video, an animated intro or an explainer full of moving type, all of it made by describing what they want to an agent that writes the code.
After watching a few of them, I started wondering about something else: is there a way to do the same thing and take it to native SwiftUI? I don’t want a video inside the app. I want a scene that’s drawn on the device, like any other view.
Because the scene is code and not an embedded video, I control things a video can’t. I can change its speed without exporting anything again. The same scene is drawn in light or dark mode colours, because it reads the app’s colours at that moment. And it can adapt to the device: on the iPhone Duo it makes no sense to show the same animation with the phone open and closed, and the clock scene, for example, shows the real hinge when the Duo is in tabletop mode. Here it is both ways:
The same clock scene on an iPhone and on an iPhone Duo in tabletop: the code decides what to draw · open in a new tab This demo needs JavaScript.
There’s another case I find even more interesting. Some people turn on Reduce Motion in Settings › Accessibility › Motion, because animations make them dizzy or distract them. Apps can read that setting (in SwiftUI, through the accessibilityReduceMotion environment value). With a video, all you can do is remove it. With a scene in code, I pick a frame that already tells the story and leave it as a still image, respecting that person’s choice.
These are the scenes in the MindChess onboarding and What’s New screen. They were born in HTML with an AI agent. Then they moved to SwiftUI without a single SwiftUI animation, no withAnimation, no matchedGeometryEffect, no transitions.
Ten coins that forge a badge, and picking a rival who plays the first move. Let’s talk about these two examples.
The idea: a scene is a function of time # The usual way to animate in SwiftUI is to declare states and let the system interpolate between them. It works very well for UI, but for a five-second scene with fifteen things moving out of step it turns into a chain of DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter, intermediate states and animations stepping on each other.
The motion graphics people make with AI don’t work like that. They’re a timeline. At 1200 ms this is here, and 300 ms later, at 1500 ms, it’s over there. So I borrowed that idea. The MindChess scenes have no state. They have a function:
draw(t) → the frame at second t Everything on screen is computed from t: where each piece is, its opacity, its size, which move has been played. Nothing depends on the previous frame.
That gives you three things for free:
Deterministic snapshot tests (tests that compare an image of the view with a saved one): drawing draw(4.4), the 4400 ms mark, always gives the same image. Reduce Motion: instead of animating, you draw a single still frame that already tells the story. Seamless loops: if everything fades back to zero opacity at the end, the first frame and the last one line up. And a fourth one, which is the one that matters here: a pure function translates from one language to another. If the prototype is a stateless JavaScript function, the Swift port is another function with the same lines.
A fixed box and a grammar # Every scene is drawn in a logical box of 360 × 280 points and then scaled to whatever space the screen gives it. That way the prototype’s coordinates and the Swift ones are the same, number for number.
And they all follow the same grammar: entry → action → result → rest. Something appears, something happens, you see the result and the scene settles on a frame that sums it up. That rest frame is the instant each scene declares as its stillTime. It’s the one drawn with Reduce Motion and in the snapshot tests, so it has to tell the story on its own.
This grammar is also what I ask the agent for. I don’t say “make me a nice animation”. I tell it what happens in each phase and at which millisecond.
Closed-form curves # For draw(t) to be pure, motion can’t come from a step-by-step simulation. Every curve is a closed-form formula you can evaluate at any instant. There are five of them, and they fit on one screen.
In JavaScript, in the prototype:
const S = (x, w = 14) => { // damped spring from 0 to 1 if (x <= 0) return 0; const z = 0.78, wd = w * Math.sqrt(1 - z * z), e = Math.exp(-z * w * x); return 1 - e * (Math.cos(wd * x) + ((z * w) / wd) * Math.sin(wd * x)); }; const clamp = (v, a = 0, b = 1) => Math.min(b, Math.max(a, v)); const smooth = (a, b, x) => { const u = clamp((x - a) / (b - a)); return u * u * (3 - 2 * u); }; const lerp = (a, b, k) => a + (b - a) * k; const bump = (t, c, len = 0.14, w = 30) => S(t - c, w) - S(t - c - len, w); And in Swift, in the app, line by line:
public enum Motion { /// Damped spring from 0 to 1 starting at `x = 0` (damping 0.78, `w` rad/s); 0 before it starts. public static func spring(_ x: Double, _ w: Double = 14) -> Double { guard x > 0 else { return 0 } let z = 0.78, wd = w * (1 - z * z).squareRoot(), e = exp(-z * w * x) return 1 - e * (cos(wd * x) + (z * w / wd) * sin(wd * x)) } public static func clamp(_ v: Double, _ a: Double = 0, _ b: Double = 1) -> Double { min(b, max(a, v)) } public static func smooth(_ a: Double, _ b: Double, _ x: Double) -> Double { let u = clamp((x - a) / (b - a)) return u * u * (3 - 2 * u) } public static func lerp(_ a: Double, _ b: Double, _ k: Double) -> Double { a + (b - a) * k } /// A spring up at `c` and back down `len` seconds later. public static func bump(_ t: Double, _ c: Double, _ len: Double = 0.14, _ w: Double = 30) -> Double { spring(t - c, w) - spring(t - c - len, w) } } spring is the response of a spring with 0.78 damping. It goes from 0 to 1, overshoots a little and settles. The w parameter sets how fast. smooth goes from 0 to 1 between two instants, easing in and out (graphics people call this curve smoothstep), perfect for fades. bump is a spring that goes up and comes back down, a “pop”.
In the demos for both cases, further down, you can change the springs’ damping and frequency and see how both the curve and the animation itself change. The dot marks where the scene’s main spring is at each instant.
Prototyping in the browser with AI # The prototype lives in the MindChess design kit, in a JavaScript file of scenes (motion.js). Each scene is a function that takes a <canvas> context and t. Writing them with an AI agent works especially well, for three reasons:
The plain-language description is almost the code already. “Ten coins on a ring of radius 88; one drops every 200 milliseconds from 64 pt above with a spring of frequency 16” translates almost literally. You iterate by looking at the browser. I reload, drag time to the moment I don’t like and tell the agent what to change at that exact instant. The data is real. The colours come from the app’s tokens, the pieces are the game’s and the avatars are the real bots'. Then the same agent does the port. I give it the JavaScript scene and the Swift kit, and since both are pure functions with the same curves, the result comes out right almost on the first try.
The SwiftUI port # The port has three parts.
A protocol for scenes. Each scene says how long it lasts, which frame is its still frame and how it’s drawn:
public protocol MotionScene: Sendable { var duration: Double { get } var stillTime: Double { get } var box: CGSize { get } // 360 × 280 by default var speed: Double { get } // 1 by default func draw(_ canvas: inout MotionCanvas, t: Double) } A canvas you copy. MotionCanvas wraps SwiftUI’s GraphicsContext (the object you draw with inside a Canvas), the colour scheme’s palette and a few helpers (circle, fill, text, image). It’s a value type (a struct: assigning it makes a copy), and that replaces the HTML canvas’s save() and restore(), which save and restore the drawing state. To change the opacity or the transform of one part, you copy it, change the copy and throw it away.
var coin = c // a copy: saves the state coin.fade(M.clamp((t - ti) * 6) * (1 - melt)) coin.circle(CGPoint(x: p.x, y: y), 10.5, accent) // when this scope ends, `c` is as it was A view that gives the scene its time. It’s a Canvas (SwiftUI’s view for drawing by hand, like an HTML <canvas>) inside a TimelineView (a view that redraws on every frame and tells you the time). It scales the 360 × 280 box to the available space and calls draw with the right t:
TimelineView(.animation(minimumInterval: 1 / 60, paused: !isLive || !isOnScreen)) { timeline in Canvas { context, size in let time = reduceMotion || isResting ? scene.stillTime : liveTime(timeline.date.timeIntervalSince(start)) draw(in: context, size: size, t: time) } } With that in place, let’s go back to the two examples from the start.
Case 1: ten coins that forge a badge # The first one is from the onboarding: every game you play is a coin, and ten coins forge your first badge. Following the grammar:
Phase Time What happens Entry 0–250 ms The ring of ten slots appears Action 350–2150 ms A coin drops every 200 ms and the counter goes up Result 2750–4000 ms The ring melts, the badge flips and is earned, sparks fly Rest 4400 ms (stillTime = 4.4) The still frame, with the badge and “10/10” The same function at five instants. At 4400 ms, the still frame. This is the real scene, running the prototype’s own JavaScript. You can pause it and scrub through time:
The badge scene in the browser: scrub through time and play with the spring · open in a new tab This demo needs JavaScript.
Drag t and you’ll see you can jump to any instant, forwards or backwards. That’s the whole idea.
This is the prototype (trimmed):
M.define('coins', { dur: 6, still: 4.4, draw(g, t, e) { const { th } = e, cx = 180, cy = 124, R = 88, FORGE = 2.75; g.globalAlpha = smooth(0, 0.25, t) * (1 - smooth(5.4, 5.9, t)); // entry and exit const melt = smooth(FORGE, FORGE + 0.3, t); for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { const a = -Math.PI / 2 + (i * Math.PI * 2) / 10, x = cx + R * Math.cos(a), y = cy + R * Math.sin(a); const ti = 0.35 + i * 0.2, k = S(t - ti, 16); if (t > ti) { g.save(); g.globalAlpha *= clamp((t - ti) * 6) * (1 - melt); const yy = lerp(y - 64, y, k); // drops from 64 pt above circle(g, x, yy, 10.5, C.accent); g.restore(); } } // …the ring melting, the badge flipping, the sparks and the counter } }); And in Swift, with the same curves and the same box, it reads the same way:
struct CoinsScene: MotionScene { var duration: Double { 6 } var stillTime: Double { 4.4 } func draw(_ c: inout MotionCanvas, t: Double) { let cx = 180.0, cy = 124.0, r = 88.0, forge = 2.75 c.fade(M.smooth(0, 0.25, t) * (1 - M.smooth(5.4, 5.9, t))) let melt = M.smooth(forge, forge + 0.3, t) for i in 0..<10 { let a = -Double.pi / 2 + Double(i) * 2 * .pi / 10 let p = CGPoint(x: cx + r * cos(a), y: cy + r * sin(a)) let ti = 0.35 + Double(i) * 0.2, k = M.spring(t - ti, 16) guard t > ti else { continue } var coin = c coin.fade(M.clamp((t - ti) * 6) * (1 - melt)) let y = M.lerp(p.y - 64, p.y, k) coin.circle(CGPoint(x: p.x, y: y), 10.5, accent) } // …the ring melting, the badge flipping, the sparks and the counter } } Case 2: pick your rival and play the first move # The second one is from 1.4, to introduce the bots. Three rivals, one per level. Sofía is picked, she sits down by the board and answers 1.e4 with 1…e5. This time there’s a real board, with pieces flying from one square to another:
Phase Time What happens Entry 0–600 ms The three cards appear, one after another Action 1350–2400 ms Sofía lights up, the other two leave, she moves to her seat and the board appears Result 2750–3900 ms 1.e4, Sofía thinks (the three dots) and answers 1…e5 Rest 4600 ms (stillTime = 4.6) The still frame, with Sofía by the board and the last move highlighted The bots scene at five instants. The avatars and pieces are the app’s. And here it is running, with the same time controls:
The bots scene: three rivals, one is picked and 1.e4 e5 is played · open in a new tab This demo needs JavaScript.
What’s interesting about this scene is how the work is split between functions. The board is a separate function, playBoard, that takes a position and a list of moves with the instant each one is played. Each move is a spring from the source square to the destination square, and the last one is highlighted in yellow, as in the app. The scene only says which moves and when:
struct BotsScene: MotionScene { let board: BoardTheme let pieces: PieceTheme let avatarStyle: BotAvatarStyle var duration: Double { 6 } var stillTime: Double { 4.6 } var speed: Double { 1.2 } func draw(_ c: inout MotionCanvas, t: Double) { let select = 1.35, move = 2.0 c.fade(M.smooth(0, 0.2, t) * (1 - M.smooth(5.45, 5.95, t))) let leave = M.smooth(select + 0.3, select + 0.75, t), m = M.spring(t - move, 9) // …Pip and Viktor come in and leave with `leave` let bk = M.spring(t - move - 0.15, 12) if bk > 0 { var table = c table.fade(bk * 1.3) table.context.translateBy(x: 0, y: 14 * (1 - bk)) playBoard(table, t: t, origin: CGPoint(x: 132, y: 40), side: 25, fen: startFEN, moves: [("e2", "e4", 2.75), ("e7", "e5", 3.65)], board: board, pieces: pieces) } // …and Sofía's card goes from 180 to 62 with the spring `m` } } Look at the three properties at the top: board, pieces and avatarStyle. In the prototype the board is green and the pieces are the default set. In the app, the scene uses the board theme, the pieces and the avatar style the user picked in Settings. That’s exactly what a video can’t do.
And speed: 1.2. The scene was designed to last six seconds, but in the app it works better if it loops in five. Instead of redoing the timings, the scene declares a speed and real time is multiplied by it.
The details that only show up in the app # Playing the scenes in the app brought up things you don’t see in the prototype:
It plays twice and then stays still. An endlessly looping animation in an onboarding is distracting and drains the battery. After two loops, the scene stops at its stillTime, which falls inside the second loop, so there’s no jump. From then on the TimelineView is paused and nothing is redrawn. Paused when off screen and hidden from VoiceOver, because it’s decorative: the text on the page already says the same thing. The tests # Since time is a parameter, an environment value can pin it:
public enum MotionPlayback: Equatable, Sendable { case live case still case time(Double) } The onboarding and What’s New snapshots draw every scene at its still frame, in light and dark, on the iPhone and in every Duo posture. If someone changes a curve and the badge is no longer centred at 4400 ms, the test fails.
Takeaways # AI isn’t just for making motion graphics videos. If you ask for the scene as a function of time, the result can be taken to native code. A function of time is easier to reason about than a chain of animations. And you can jump to any instant to debug it. Closed-form formulas travel well between languages. The JavaScript curves and the Swift ones are the same lines in a different syntax, and the same agent does the port. Prototyping in the browser with an agent is very fast when you can point at a specific instant and say what’s wrong. Accessibility and tests come for free if the still frame tells the story. summary: Everyone is making motion graphics with AI for videos. I wanted the same thing inside the app, in native SwiftUI. The key was writing every scene as a draw(t) function.
title: MindChess onboarding animations in SwiftUI, thanks to AI

content:
In the previous article we stored a chess board in memory with bitboards. This one covers the other half: drawing it on screen with SwiftUI, in a way that holds up to everything a chess app throws at it.
The board shows up almost everywhere in MindChess: puzzles, repertoire, the game viewer, the opening explorer, the GIF creator… Every one of those screens uses the same board view, and each wants something different. One lets only one side move, another lets nobody move, another animates more slowly so you can follow the reply. One view can cover all of that thanks to three decisions:
Layers stacked in a ZStack, all placed with the same geometry function. Layers grouped by what makes them change, so a move, a tap or a drag only redraws what it has to. A TCA State and Action built around the gesture: the view reports what the person did, the board applies the rules, and the parent screen decides what it means. The code here is a rewritten, trimmed-down version of what the app uses. Both complete files are linked at the end.
MindChessThe board from this post, on your iPhone
Train board vision, memory and calculation in 60-second drills, sharpen your tactics and study your own games.
One geometry function # Before any layers, one rule: everything drawn on the board is placed with the same function. Squares, pieces, highlights, legal-move dots, arrows. If each layer did its own math, sooner or later one would drift by half a pixel, especially once you flip the board.
extension Square { func center(squareSize: CGFloat, orientation: Orientation) -> CGPoint { let column = orientation == .white ? file : 7 - file let row = orientation == .white ? 7 - rank : rank return CGPoint(x: (CGFloat(column) + 0.5) * squareSize, y: (CGFloat(row) + 0.5) * squareSize) } } With Black at the bottom, column and row are flipped, and that’s it. No layer knows the board is upside down. The inverse function, point to square, is what the drag gesture uses to find the square under your finger.
Every layer places its views with .position(square.center(…)). position puts the view’s center at that point, which is exactly what the function returns. On the outside, .aspectRatio(1, contentMode: .fit) plus min(width, height) / 8 keep the board square and let it fit any space: iPhone, iPad, Mac, or half the screen of a foldable.
The eight layers # The board is a ZStack of eight layers. Bottom to top:
The eight layers of the board. The color shows each layer’s group, based on what makes it change. Squares. All 64, each at its center. Last move. From and to squares highlighted. Selected square. The piece you just tapped. Square under the finger. While dragging, the square you would drop on. Check. A red glow under the king, only when in check. Pieces. Legal moves. A dot on every square the selected piece can reach. NAG. The !, ?, ??… badge of the move, on its destination square. In the view, each layer is one line of the ZStack:
ZStack { BackgroundLayer(store: store.scope(state: \.background, action: \.background), …) // 1 lastMove(squareSize: squareSize) // 2 .animation(nil, value: store.game) selection(squareSize: squareSize) // 3 and 4 check(squareSize: squareSize) // 5 PiecesLayer(store: store.scope(state: \.pieces, action: \.pieces), …) // 6 .allowsHitTesting(configuration.movableSides.contains(store.game.turn)) legalMoves(squareSize: squareSize) // 7 nag(squareSize: squareSize) // 8 } .frame(width: side, height: side) The order matters. Highlights sit below the pieces because they color the square, not the piece. Legal-move dots sit above because they are buttons as well as dots: if you capture by tapping the dot on top of an enemy piece, the tap has to reach the dot, not the piece. The NAG badge goes on top of everything so nothing ever covers it.
Each layer can also be switched on or off by a board configuration. A puzzle doesn’t need NAGs; the game viewer doesn’t need legal-move dots. Adding something new, like engine arrows, means slotting a layer in the right place without touching the others.
Why some layers belong together # Eight layers doesn’t mean eight independent things. Look at what makes each layer change and you get four groups. That grouping is what decides how things animate and how much gets redrawn:
Background (layer 1): only changes with the board theme or the coordinates. Game (layers 2, 5 and 8): change when a move is played. Interaction (layers 3, 4 and 7): change at the pace of the gesture. Pieces (layer 6): change with the move, and are the only thing that animates. What redraws when something happens. The background has its own store # The 64 squares live in a child view with its own scope of the store, and that view only reads the theme:
struct BackgroundLayer: View { let store: StoreOf<BackgroundFeature> let orientation: Orientation let squareSize: CGFloat var body: some View { SquaresLayer(theme: store.theme, orientation: orientation, squareSize: squareSize) } } With @ObservableState, SwiftUI re-evaluates a view’s body only when something that view read has changed. The board as a whole changes on every move, every tap and every square your finger crosses, but the background never read any of that, so its 64 views are left alone. It only hears about a theme change in Settings.
Pieces: one group, one animation # The pieces are a ForEach inside their own ZStack, with a single animation modifier:
ZStack { ForEach(pieces) { piece in let isDragged = piece.square == drag?.square PieceView(piece: piece, …, dragTranslation: isDragged ? drag?.translation : nil) .zIndex(isDragged ? 1 : 0) .onTapGesture { store.send(.delegate(.userTap(on: piece.square))) } .gesture(dragGesture(from: piece.square)) } } .animation(.snappy(duration: animationDuration), value: pieces) Grouping them like this buys three things:
A move is one transaction. Castling moves the king and the rook; a capture slides one piece and removes another. Because every piece hangs off the same .animation(value: pieces), all of it happens in one animation, with one curve and one duration. No piece arrives before the others. zIndex works. zIndex only orders siblings within the same container. Since all the pieces are siblings, the one you drag rises above the rest. If each piece lived in a different layer, there would be no way to lift it. The animation stays contained. The modifier sits on the pieces group, not on the whole board, so nothing else animates by accident. The duration comes from the configuration: repertoire boards animate more slowly so the opponent’s reply is easy to follow. For SwiftUI to slide a piece instead of tearing it down and building a new one, each piece needs a stable identity: the g1 knight is still the same knight after it jumps to f3. In MindChess the engine keeps an identifier per piece, moves it along with the piece on every move, and restores it on undo. If the id were the square, every move would read as “a view disappears from g1 and another appears on f3”, and there would be nothing to animate.
The last move jumps, it doesn’t slide # The last-move highlights depend on the game just like the pieces do. If the parent screen changes the game inside a withAnimation (stepping through the game viewer, say), those two yellow squares would slide from the previous move to the new one, trailing behind the pieces. It looks wrong. So that layer gets:
lastMove(squareSize: squareSize) .animation(nil, value: store.game) Now the highlights are simply in place while the piece slides. The NAG badge gets the same result with a different tool: an .id(…) that changes with every move, so SwiftUI treats it as a new view instead of moving it from the previous square.
Pieces that don’t move aren’t redrawn # Each piece is a small view that only takes values:
struct PieceView: View, Equatable { let piece: BoardPiece let style: PieceStyle let position: CGPoint let squareSize: CGFloat let dragTranslation: CGSize? … } While you drag, only one piece’s dragTranslation changes. The other 31 get exactly the same values as before, and SwiftUI skips their body. This went from nice-to-have to essential because of dragging.
Dragging, or what a mouse taught me # The first version kept the drag offset in the TCA store. Every DragGesture event sent actions with the new offset, and on iPhone it felt fine.
Then I tried it on the Mac with a mouse, and the piece trailed behind the pointer. I measured it: a mouse can send up to about 1,200 events per second (a trackpad, about 150). Each event sent four actions through the reducer tree from the root and redrew every piece, at 3–5 ms per event. The main thread couldn’t keep up.
Dragging, before and after. The fix was to separate where the finger is from what the person means. The offset lives in a @State of the pieces view; the store only hears what it cares about:
struct PieceDrag: Equatable { let square: Square var translation: CGSize = .zero var targetSquare: Square? /// Follows the finger and returns an action only when the square underneath changes. mutating func move(translation: CGSize, over target: Square?) -> PiecesFeature.Action.Delegate? { self.translation = translation guard let target, target != targetSquare else { return nil } targetSquare = target return .userDragging(on: target) } } Now dragging from g1 to f3 is a handful of actions: one on start, one per square crossed, one on drop. Every other event only touches the @State, which only redraws the moving piece.
One last detail: on drop, the piece is already sitting on its target square. If the game change were animated, SwiftUI would snap it back to the origin and slide it again. So the end of the gesture turns animations off for that transaction:
var transaction = Transaction() transaction.disablesAnimations = true withTransaction(transaction) { drag = nil if let target { store.send(.delegate(.userEndDragging(on: target))) } } A reader’s note # After the post went out, a reader left this reply on X:
Keep pointer position local, but send a completed move through the same legality check as tap, keyboard, and VoiceOver. A canceled drag should leave both board and move history unchanged. Otherwise the mouse path becomes a second rules engine.
— Vitaliy Podolskiy (@onlyapps_org) November 2, 2026 Spot on, and it’s exactly the split the change above was after. The offset lives in the view’s @State, but dropping a piece (userEndDragging) and tapping a legal-move dot (legalTargetTapped) both end in the same play function, the only place a move reaches the game, and always after isLegal. When the board supports keyboard and VoiceOver, those inputs will have to send the same actions; that’s a topic for another post.
The canceled drag is the part I didn’t tell. In MindChess, if you release the piece outside the board, the selection clears and the game and its history stay the same. But the post didn’t explain it, and the simplified sample code had left it out: with target set to nil nothing was sent, so selectedSquare and draggedSquare stayed set and the highlight stuck on screen. This is how the app handles it, and now the sample does too: the gesture reports the cancel and the board clears the selection.
// PiecesFeature.Action.Delegate case userEndDragging(on: Square) case userCancelDragging // DragGesture.onEnded if let target { store.send(.delegate(.userEndDragging(on: target))) } else { store.send(.delegate(.userCancelDragging)) } // BoardFeature case .pieces(.delegate(.userCancelDragging)): state.clearSelection() return .none Thanks for reading it so carefully: that’s how these posts get better.
Board State and Action in TCA # With the layers settled: what goes in the store, and what doesn’t? My rule is: State holds what decides what gets drawn; the view holds what only describes how the gesture looks.
Who decides what: view, board and parent screen. State # @ObservableState struct State: Equatable { var game = Game.initial var orientation: Orientation = .white var background = BackgroundFeature.State() // theme and coordinates var pieces = PiecesFeature.State() // piece style var selectedSquare: Square? var legalTargets: Set<Square> = [] var draggedSquare: Square? } game is the source of truth: pieces, last move, check and side to move all come from it. selectedSquare, legalTargets and draggedSquare feed the interaction layers. In the app, legal moves are a bitboard (like the ones in the previous article), turned into squares when drawn. background and pieces are the state of two child features. Splitting them out is what lets the background observe only the theme. The app keeps two more things for promotion: the pending move and a @Presents var destination for the piece picker sheet. Plus the NAGs of the current move, which layer 8 draws. Just as important is what isn’t in State:
The drag offset, for the reasons above. The board configuration: which layers are drawn, which sides can move, how long the animation takes. That’s a per-screen decision, not state that changes, so it lives in the view: struct BoardConfiguration: Equatable, Sendable { var movableSides: Set<PieceColor> var pieceAnimationDuration: Double var showsLastMove: Bool var showsSelection: Bool var showsLegalMoves: Bool } BoardView(store: store, configuration: .viewer) The app has ready-made configurations for each screen: puzzle, PGN viewer, learning and practicing a repertoire… Repertoire practice, for instance, animates in 0.55 s instead of 0.18 s.
Action # The board’s actions read best grouped by who sends them:
enum Action: Sendable { // Commands from the parent screen case setGame(Game) case setOrientation(Orientation) // Child features case background(BackgroundFeature.Action) case pieces(PiecesFeature.Action) // From this view case legalTargetTapped(Square) // To the parent screen case delegate(Delegate) @CasePathable enum Delegate: Sendable { case userMoved(Move) } } The pieces feature never moves anything. It only reports what happened, through delegate actions: userTap, userStartDragging, userDragging (once per square) and userEndDragging. The board decides:
case let .pieces(.delegate(.userTap(on: square))), let .pieces(.delegate(.userStartDragging(on: square))): state.select(square) return .none case let .pieces(.delegate(.userDragging(on: square))): state.draggedSquare = square return .none case let .pieces(.delegate(.userEndDragging(on: square))), let .legalTargetTapped(square): return play(&state, to: square) And play is the only place where a move becomes part of the game:
private func play(_ state: inout State, to square: Square) -> Effect<Action> { defer { state.clearSelection() } guard let from = state.selectedSquare else { return .none } let move = Move(from: from, to: square) guard state.game.isLegal(move) else { return .none } state.game.execute(move) return .send(.delegate(.userMoved(move))) } If the move isn’t legal, the game doesn’t change and the piece goes back to its square by itself, because its position always comes from game. In the app, this same spot also plays the move sound (a dependency) and, when a pawn reaches the last rank, presents the promotion sheet instead of executing the move.
Why a delegate for the parent # The parent screen could observe game and react when it changes. But game changes for many reasons: a setGame on load, the engine’s reply, an undo… The userMoved delegate says something more specific: the person made this move. With that, each screen does its own thing and the board knows nothing about it:
case let .board(.delegate(.userMoved(move))): // Puzzle: is this the move we were looking for? // Game against the engine: time to reply. // Repertoire: is it in your line? The board has no idea whether it’s in a puzzle or the viewer. It only knows chess and gestures.
What I’d do differently # Think in groups from day one. The layers arrived one by one, and the grouping (what animates, what jumps, what each view observes) came later, when something broke. It’s easier to decide as you add each layer. Keep anything continuous out of the store. The drag in the store worked on iPhone and broke on the Mac. The rule now is simple: if it changes 60+ times a second and isn’t a decision, it goes in @State. Fold the selection into one value. selectedSquare and the legal moves always travel together; a single optional selection: (square, targets)? would rule out half-set states. Measure before optimizing. 64 views for the squares are fine on an interactive board. For thumbnails in a game list I use Canvas, which draws without one view per square, but only because I measured it. The full code # Board.swift: model, geometry and layers in plain SwiftUI, no dependencies. BoardFeature.swift: the TCA features (background, pieces and board), the layered view and the drag in @State, with an Xcode preview. The rules are a toy (you can move to any square without one of your own pieces) so the example stays about drawing. Real legal moves, promotion and TestStore tests come in the next articles of the series.
If you want to see the board in action, it’s in MindChess, in every puzzle and every game you open.
summary: Eight layers, four groups, and a drag gesture that stopped going through the store. This is how the MindChess board is built with SwiftUI and TCA.
title: Anatomy of a chess board in SwiftUI: layers, animations and TCA

content:
For a while now I’ve been working on connecting two fields I’m really interested in: Swift programming and chess.
As is well known, these two worlds have been linked since the early days of computing: from Claude Shannon’s early work on chess as a computational problem, through the era of iconic machines like Deep Blue facing Kasparov, to the present with engines like Stockfish.
In this article we will dive into one of the fundamental concepts of any modern chess engine or library: bitboards.
The explanation is based on three pillars:
The classic definition described in ChessProgramming Wiki The first Swift implementation I found on the topic, which I used as a reference: Sage The implementation this article is based on (link) The goal is not only to understand what a bitboard is, but why this approach is so powerful when we work with chess logic.
What is a Bitboard? # A bitboard is, conceptually, a 64-bit integer (UInt64) where each bit represents a square on the chessboard.
Since the board has exactly 64 squares (8×8), the fit is perfect:
1 bit = 1 square Bit 1 → there is something on that square Bit 0 → the square is empty The square order relative to the bit is represented in the following image: For example, if we wanted to represent the position of all the white pawns in this image: We would mark occupied squares with a 1 and order them as shown before, resulting in the following number Why not use an 8×8 matrix? # The most intuitive way to represent a board is something like:
[[Piece?]] // 8x8 This works, but it has several problems when we want performance:
Indirect memory access Many conditions (if, guard) Hard to calculate attacks in bulk Poor CPU utilization Bitboards, on the other hand, allow:
Operations in a single instruction Heavy use of bitwise operations (&, |, ^, <<, >>) Parallel calculation of moves and attacks In chess, where every move counts, that makes a huge difference.
A board as a set of bitboards # A key idea is that there is not just one bitboard, but several.
For a position on a board we need to represent different piece types:
8 white pawns (we already saw how to represent them with a single bitboard). 2 white rooks. 2 white knights. 2 white bishops. The white king. The white queen. The equivalent for the black pieces. So with 12 bitboards we have what we need to represent a full board position.
Our implementation: Bitboard as a domain type # In the library we do not use UInt64 directly everywhere. Instead, we encapsulate the concept in a dedicated type:
public struct Bitboard { private(set) var rawValue: UInt64 } This has several advantages:
Strong typing (we do not mix “normal” integers with bitboards) Expressive API Safety and readability Ability to add chess-specific behavior A Bitboard is not a number, it is a domain concept.
Bitwise operations as the language of chess # With the 12 bitboards defined we can answer questions like:
Which squares are occupied? Which squares are free? Which squares does this piece attack? Everything is built on binary operations.
OR (|) – union # Thinking of bitboards as the set of the 12 bitboards of a position, we get the set of occupied squares like this:
public var occupiedSpaces: Bitboard { return bitboards.reduce(0, |) } NOT (~) – complement # Once we have the occupied squares, it is easy to detect the empty ones as the complement:
public var emptySpaces: Bitboard { return ~occupiedSpaces } We can implement all the binary logical operators we want, here is an example:
extension Bitboard { public static func << (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { let shifted = lhs.rawValue << rhs.rawValue return Bitboard(rawValue: shifted) } public static func >> (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { let shifted = lhs.rawValue >> rhs.rawValue return Bitboard(rawValue: shifted) } public static func <<= (lhs: inout Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) { lhs = lhs << rhs } public static func >>= (lhs: inout Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) { lhs = lhs >> rhs } public static func & (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { Bitboard(rawValue: lhs.rawValue & rhs.rawValue) } public static func | (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { Bitboard(rawValue: lhs.rawValue | rhs.rawValue) } public static func ^ (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { Bitboard(rawValue: lhs.rawValue ^ rhs.rawValue) } public static func > (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bool { lhs.rawValue > rhs.rawValue } public static func < (lhs: Bitboard, rhs: Bitboard) -> Bool { lhs.rawValue < rhs.rawValue } public static prefix func ~ (board: Bitboard) -> Bitboard { Bitboard(rawValue: ~board.rawValue) } } Iterating squares: popcount and bit scan # Another key point is iterating only over active squares, not all 64.
Instead of:
for square in 0..<64 We use techniques like:
popcount → number of active bits extracting the least significant bit clearing the bit once processed In our implementation, the Bitboard iterator does exactly that: it keeps popping the LS1B (least significant set bit) with popLSB() until the board is empty. Internally we use the classic trick described in BitScan:
extension Bitboard { /// A lookup table of least significant bit indices. private static let lsbTable: [Int] = [00, 01, 48, 02, 57, 49, 28, 03, 61, 58, 50, 42, 38, 29, 17, 04, 62, 55, 59, 36, 53, 51, 43, 22, 45, 39, 33, 30, 24, 18, 12, 05, 63, 47, 56, 27, 60, 41, 37, 16, 54, 35, 52, 21, 44, 32, 23, 11, 46, 26, 40, 15, 34, 20, 31, 10, 25, 14, 19, 09, 13, 08, 07, 06] /// A lookup table of most significant bit indices. private static let msbTable: [Int] = [00, 47, 01, 56, 48, 27, 02, 60, 57, 49, 41, 37, 28, 16, 03, 61, 54, 58, 35, 52, 50, 42, 21, 44, 38, 32, 29, 23, 17, 11, 04, 62, 46, 55, 26, 59, 40, 36, 15, 53, 34, 51, 20, 43, 31, 22, 10, 45, 25, 39, 14, 33, 19, 30, 09, 24, 13, 18, 08, 12, 07, 06, 05, 63] /// A lookup table of bitboards for all squares. private static let bitboardTable: [Bitboard] = (0 ..< 64).map { Bitboard(rawValue: 1 << $0) } /// The De Bruijn multiplier. private static let debruijn64: UInt64 = 0x03f79d71b4cb0a89 /// Returns the index of the lsb value. private func index(lsb value: Bitboard) -> Int? { guard value != 0 else { return nil } return Bitboard.lsbTable[Int((value.rawValue &* Bitboard.debruijn64) >> 58)] } /// The least significant bit. public var lsb: Bitboard { return Bitboard(rawValue: rawValue & (0 &- rawValue)) } /// The index for the least significant bit of `self`. public var lsbIndex: Int? { return index(lsb: lsb) } /// The square for the least significant bit of `self`. public var lsbSquare: Square? { return lsbIndex.flatMap({ Square(rawValue: $0) }) } private var msbShifted: UInt64 { var x = rawValue x |= x >> 1 x |= x >> 2 x |= x >> 4 x |= x >> 8 x |= x >> 16 x |= x >> 32 return x } /// The most significant bit. public var msb: Bitboard { return Bitboard(rawValue: (msbShifted >> 1) + 1) } /// The index for the most significant bit of `self`. public var msbIndex: Int? { guard rawValue != 0 else { return nil } return Bitboard.msbTable[Int((msbShifted &* Bitboard.debruijn64) >> 58)] } /// The square for the most significant bit of `self`. public var msbSquare: Square? { return msbIndex.flatMap({ Square(rawValue: $0) }) } /// Removes the least significant bit and returns it. public mutating func popLSB() -> Bitboard { let lsb = self.lsb rawValue -= lsb.rawValue return lsb } /// Removes the least significant bit and returns its index, if any. public mutating func popLSBIndex() -> Int? { return index(lsb: popLSB()) } /// Removes the least significant bit and returns its square, if any. public mutating func popLSBSquare() -> Square? { return popLSBIndex().flatMap({ Square(rawValue: $0) }) } } lsb = x & -x with this operation we isolate the least significant active bit (the 1 that is lowest in the binary number) Thanks to the De Bruijn tables and the private func index(lsb value: Bitboard) -> Int? function we can get the index to know the square We call popLSB to remove that bit and continue iterating. public struct Bitboard: Equatable, Hashable { private(set) var rawValue: UInt64 = 0 public init(rawValue: UInt64) { self.rawValue = rawValue } public init() {} /// An iterator over the squares set in a `Bitboard`. /// /// Iterates by popping least significant bits until the bitboard is empty. public struct Iterator: IteratorProtocol { fileprivate var bitboard: Bitboard /// Returns the next square in the bitboard by removing the least significant bit. public mutating func next() -> Square? { return bitboard.popLSBSquare() } } } This greatly reduces the computational cost, especially for move generation, because we only walk the squares with pieces instead of all 64.
Conclusion # Bitboards are not just an optimization:
they are a different way to think about chess in code.
By representing the board as binary data:
Chess becomes algebra Moves become operations The position becomes a compact, efficient state In upcoming articles we will see how to generate attack bitboards for each piece, build complete positions, and legal move generation from this base.
title: Bitboards: Representing the Chessboard Efficiently

Intro # Publish is an awesome static site generator created by John Sundell. This website is built with this tool.
One of the steps is to upload to the server all the file generated, the first approach I used was to upload all the files in the output folder, via FTP manually but, then I had an idea.
Deploy # For deployment, I use the following code:
.publish( withTheme: .nsstudent, deployedUsing: DeploymentMethod.gitHub("NSStudent/NSStudent"), ... } This is the implementation of the github method:
/// Deploy a website to a given GitHub repository. /// - parameter repository: The full name of the repository (including its username). /// - parameter useSSH: Whether an SSH connection should be used (preferred). static func gitHub(_ repository: String, useSSH: Bool = true) -> Self { let prefix = useSSH ? "git@github.com:" : "https://github.com/" return git("\(prefix)\(repository).git") } This method searches the repository with the name NSStudent/NSStudent. By default, the implementation tries to clone the repository via SSH with this code inside the git method.
static func git(_ remote: String) -> Self { DeploymentMethod(name: "Git (\(remote))") { context in let folder = try context.createDeploymentFolder(withPrefix: "Git") { folder in if !folder.containsSubfolder(named: ".git") { try shellOut(to: .gitInit(), at: folder.path) try shellOut( to: "git remote add origin \(remote)", at: folder.path ) } try shellOut( to: "git remote set-url origin \(remote)", at: folder.path ) _ = try? shellOut( to: .gitPull(remote: "origin", branch: "master"), at: folder.path ) try folder.empty() } let dateFormatter = DateFormatter() dateFormatter.dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm" let dateString = dateFormatter.string(from: Date()) do { try shellOut( to: """ git add . && git commit -a -m \"Publish deploy \(dateString)\" --allow-empty """, at: folder.path ) try shellOut( to: .gitPush(remote: "origin", branch: "master"), at: folder.path ) } catch let error as ShellOutError { throw PublishingError(infoMessage: error.message) } catch { throw error } } } The magic happens when the context calls context.createDeploymentFolder function. This method creates a new folder with the name GitDeploy inside to a hidden folder .publish.
Right now, all the codes are in your repository.
To create the action to upload the website in the server via FTP, you need to add the following main.yml file:
name: Deploy website on: [push] jobs: FTP-Deploy-Action: name: FTP-Deploy-Action runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@master - name: FTP-Deploy-Action uses: SamKirkland/FTP-Deploy-Action@2.0.0 env: FTP_SERVER: ${{ secrets.FTP_NAME }} FTP_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.FTP_USER }} FTP_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.FTP_PASSWORD }} ARGS: --delete --exclude-glob=.git*/** --exclude-glob=.git** --delete-excluded This file use the FTP-Deploy-Action. It has three secrets variables secrets.FTP_NAME, secrets.FTP_USER, secrets.FTP_PASSWORD to not expose the real values. The ARGS parameter tries to remove all unused files and it prevents the upload off all the files inside the .git or .github folders.
You need to pull this change in the current GitDeploy repository. Right now, every time you use Publish deploy in the terminal and push a new version in this repository, the action uploads all the files to the FTP.
I will try to write with new things about Publish and how I use them in this blog.
title: Deploy Publish blog with Github Actions

content:
Introducción # Hugo es un generador de sitios estáticos rápido y flexible que permite crear y personalizar blogs de manera sencilla. Publicar tu blog en GitHub Pages es una excelente manera de alojarlo de forma gratuita y con alta disponibilidad. En esta guía, aprenderás a crear un blog con Hugo y publicarlo en GitHub Pages paso a paso.
Prerrequisitos # Antes de comenzar, asegúrate de tener lo siguiente:
Git instalado en tu máquina. Hugo instalado. Una cuenta en GitHub. Crear tu Blog con Hugo # Inicializar un Nuevo Proyecto de Hugo
Crea un directorio para tu blog e inicializa el proyecto:
mkdir MiBlog cd MiBlog hugo new site . Elegir un Tema
Busca un tema que te guste en Hugo Themes y clónalo en tu proyecto:
git init git submodule add https://github.com/<autor>/<tema>.git themes/<tema> echo 'theme = "<tema>"' >> config.toml Crear tu Primer Artículo
Genera un archivo de contenido:
hugo new posts/mi-primer-articulo.md Edita el archivo creado en content/posts/mi-primer-articulo.md y agrega contenido relevante.
Previsualizar el Blog Localmente
Inicia el servidor de desarrollo para ver tu blog en el navegador:
hugo server Abre http://localhost:1313 en tu navegador para ver tu blog.
Publicar en GitHub Pages # Crear un Repositorio en GitHub
Ve a GitHub y crea un nuevo repositorio. Anota la URL del repositorio.
Configurar el Repositorio Local
Conecta tu proyecto a GitHub:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<tu-usuario>/<repositorio>.git Configurar la Rama para Publicación
Hugo genera los archivos del sitio estático en el directorio public. Configuraremos esta carpeta como la rama gh-pages:
hugo cd public git init git remote add origin https://github.com/<tu-usuario>/<repositorio>.git git checkout -b gh-pages git add . git commit -m "Publicar sitio inicial" git push origin gh-pages --force Configurar GitHub Pages
Ve a la configuración del repositorio en GitHub, selecciona Pages, y elige la rama gh-pages como fuente.
Automatizar Publicaciones (Opcional)
Puedes configurar GitHub Actions para automatizar la publicación cada vez que hagas un cambio:
Crea un archivo .github/workflows/deploy.yml: name: Deploy Hugo Site on: push: branches: - main jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v3 with: submodules: true - name: Setup Hugo uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v2 with: hugo-version: 'latest' - name: Build run: hugo - name: Deploy uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3 with: github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} publish_dir: ./public Realiza un commit y haz un push del archivo. Extra: Publicar en el github-page del usuario con un Submódulo # Si quieres usar el repositorio especial <User>.github.io para alojar tu blog, puedes configurar la carpeta public como un submódulo. Este método permite que tu código fuente y los archivos generados del sitio estén separados, manteniendo el repositorio principal limpio.
Pasos: # Crear el Repositorio Especial
Ve a GitHub y crea un repositorio con el nombre exacto <User>.github.io.
Configurar el Submódulo para public
Desde la raíz de tu proyecto Hugo, añade el repositorio como submódulo vinculado a la carpeta public:
git submodule add -b main https://github.com/<User>/<User>.github.io.git public Generar el Sitio Estático
Construye el sitio estático de Hugo, que generará los archivos en la carpeta public:
hugo Publicar los Archivos en <User>.github.io
Navega a la carpeta public, agrega y realiza un commit de los archivos generados, y luego súbelos al repositorio remoto:
cd public git add . git commit -m "Publicar sitio inicial" git push origin main cd .. Guardar el Código Fuente del Blog
Vuelve al repositorio principal (el directorio raíz de tu proyecto Hugo) y realiza un commit de los cambios relacionados con el submódulo:
git add . git commit -m "Configurar submódulo para publicar en GitHub Pages" git push origin main Configurar GitHub Pages
GitHub detectará automáticamente el contenido publicado en el repositorio <User>.github.io y lo servirá desde https://<User>.github.io.
Notas: # Cada vez que realices cambios en tu blog y generes los archivos estáticos, deberás navegar a la carpeta public, hacer un commit y un push para actualizar tu sitio. Si deseas automatizar este proceso, puedes configurar un script o usar GitHub Actions. Esta opción es ideal si prefieres que tu blog esté alojado en el dominio principal de GitHub Pages (<User>.github.io) en lugar de un subdirectorio.
Conclusión # ¡Eso es todo! Ahora tienes un blog funcional en Hugo alojado gratuitamente en GitHub Pages. Puedes personalizarlo, agregar más artículos y compartir tu contenido con el mundo. Si necesitas más ayuda, consulta la documentación oficial de Hugo y GitHub Pages.
title: Crear un Blog con Hugo y Publicarlo en GitHub Pages

content:
Structs create a default initializer when you implement one.
Sometimes you want to create another initializer to facilitate the code.
The problems appear when you try to introduce our initializer. the default constructor disappears. To avoid this problem, the best way is to include our initializer inside an extension.
This way, we’ll keep the two builders
struct Person { let name: String let birthday: Date } extension Person { init(name: String) { self.name = name self.birthday = Date() } } let person = Person(name: "NSStudent", birthday: Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 426348250)) let baby = Person(name: "john")
title: Create a custom struct initializer

content:
Introducción # Normalmente, cuando desarrollamos, intentamos hacer nuestro código reutilizable. Muchas cosas que hacemos en nuestros proyectos son comunes, conectarte a una API, cachear las imágenes de la red, etc.
Para poder manejar estos recursos normalmente hacemos uso de gestores de dependencias pero, para el desarrollo en iOS, no teníamos un gestor facilitado por Apple. Hasta hace bien poco la mayoría de los desarrolladores estábamos usando Cocoapods(poner link) o Carthage(poner link) para poder cubrir esta necesidad.
Con Swift Package Manager (SPM) Apple intenta dar solución a esta demanda de los desarrolladores y en la última session de la WWDC han incluido cosas que hace a SPM un posible candidato para la gestión de dependencias en producción.
Mientras estás desarrollando tu dependencia una de las necesidades es poder modificar el código en tiempo de desarrollo dentro del proyecto. Apple no deja muy claro en su documentación como hacer esto, veamos paso por paso como poderlo hacer.
Ejemplo # El primer paso seria crear el package, para ello crea una carpeta en la ruta donde quieras hacer el ejemplo y dentro de esta carpeta ejecuta la inicialización del package.
mkdir PackageExample cd PackageExample swift package init Para este tutorial vamos a crear el proyecto nuevo al que queremos incluir este package a la misma altura que la carpeta contenedora, esta seria la estructura de la carpeta actualmente.
Carpeta Contenedora - ExampleProject - PackageExample El siguiente paso es arrastrar la carpeta del package en el proyecto
Un detalle importante para que todo funcione es que no puedes tener abierto el package en el Xcode, de lo contrario no te mostrará la jerarquía de archivos al arrastrarlo.
El último paso que nos falta para que todo funcione es conectar la librería con el proyecto, esto se hace en la sección de Build Phases del proyecto en el apartado de Link Binary With Libraries, le damos al botón de + y seleccionamos la librería de nuestro package.
Con esto ya podras hacer el import de tu package en el proyecto y modificar el código a tu gusto.
title: Trabajar con Packages en local

Hi, everyone!
My name is Omar, but I’m known as NSStudent. I’m an iOS developer from Madrid, Spain.
When I have time, I like to go to NSCoder meetups to share knowledge with all developers from Madrid. One of the things that impressed me the most, when I started as an iOS developer, was the good atmosphere in the iOS community.
This is my personal website, blog and lab to test all new features of Swift.
MindChess # MindChess is my iOS app: a daily chess gym and study companion. You train board vision, memory and calculation in 60-second drills, sharpen your tactics, play bots with their own style, and bring your Lichess and Chess.com games in to see what to improve. It’s built with SwiftUI and The Composable Architecture, and a good part of what I write here comes from building it.
Website: mindchess.app Download it on the App Store Libraries # These are some of the open source Swift libraries I maintain. fischer-core is the chess core that powers MindChess.
NSStudent/fischer-core FischerCore is a Swift library that encapsulates the core logic and data structures necessary for building chess games. Named in honor of the legendary chess grandmaster Bobby Fischer, this library provides a comprehensive foundation for creating, managing, and enforcing the rules of chess. Swift 7 0 NSStudent/EasyLinkSwiftSDK Modern Swift SDK for Chessnut electronic chessboards with Bluetooth discovery, async board updates, LED control, and Swift 6 concurrency safety. Swift 3 0 NSStudent/TearKit SwiftUI + Metal package for interactive edge-tear effects, with a TearKitDemo app showing configurable cut direction, progress callbacks, and break/recover behavior. Swift 100 6 NSStudent/JevSwiftSDK An independent, type-safe Swift SDK for TypeSafe Jev, with async/await, batching, retries, and SPM support. Swift 8 0 If you want to talk to me more, you can contact with me via Twitter
Cheers!
